newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian force allowed to leave Rwanda airport.
newsitem.headline: Canadian force allowed to leave Rwanda airport.

text.p: Rwandan authorities let the Canadian vanguard of a planned international force for Zaire out of Kigali airport on Sunday after delaying them most of the day.

A Canadian embassy official said the 34 Canadians, who had arrived on three Hercules C-130 military transport planes, were allowed to leave the airport grounds with their weapons, but were told to report to Rwanda's defence ministry headquarters on Monday.
The official said, however, the scheduled arrival in Kigali on Monday of three other C-130s and an Airbus carrying 120 more Canadian troops would probably have to be delayed.

The U.N. Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of the Canadian-led force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reaches Hutu refugees flooding back to Rwanda from Zaire after two years of exile.
But since the exodus began on Friday, Rwanda's government has said the force is no longer needed.

"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," Rwandan presidential spokesman Joseph Bideri told Reuters.
During the standoff at Kigali airport, Rwandan authorities refused to let the Canadians move around with weapons on grounds the United Nations had not arranged clearance.
The Canadians would not leave their equipment unguarded and an embassy official said "if worst came to worst" they would repack the aircraft and fly out.
Major Rod Babuik, head of the Canadian contingent, earlier told Reuters between 500-700 personnel would be based in Kigali as part of the Canadian-led U.N. multinational intervention force.
"The situation is very fluid, the movement of the refugees has had a big impact on what is happening, but we have just to carry on with our plan which is to 'recce' out sites," he said.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States and its allies might modify the plan, but U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said such a force was still needed in troubled eastern Zaire.

"I can see the need for such a force...Don't think only of what you see on the television screens. There is a huge number of refugees that are absolutely invisible but are still very much in eastern Zaire," Chretien said in a BBC radio interview.
